title: MCP Static Scanner Validation Survey
subtitle: Human Evaluation of MCP Tool and Resource Risk
intro:
This study evaluates a static risk-scanning approach for Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools — the layer that lets an AI agent use services such as Google Calendar, GitHub and Slack.

You will score MCP servers on three things, one at a time: **Action Impact** (what one call can do), **Asset Confidentiality** (how harmful it would be if the information were exposed), and **Consequence Scope** (how far the result of one call can reach). Score each one separately — each section says what to ignore. A last short section asks which **inputs** of a few tools can change the risk of a call.

If a question does not make sense to you, choose **Not sure** rather than guessing. That is a useful answer.
consent: I understand the purpose of the study and agree that my anonymized responses may be used for research and evaluation of the proposed risk-scoring method.

impact.label: No Material Effect
impact.meaning: Does not read meaningful content or change meaningful state.

impact.label: Metadata
impact.meaning: Can read or change descriptive information without reading or changing the main content.
examples: Reads names, IDs, counts, timestamps, or status.
Changes a label, flag, or other descriptive field.

impact.label: Content Access / Limited Change
impact.meaning: Can read content or make a limited change.
examples: Reads the content of an item.
Changes part of an item without replacing it.

impact.label: Major Change
impact.meaning: Can create or make a major change to data, permissions, configuration, or system state, but the change can normally be reversed.

impact.label: Irreversible / Consequential
impact.meaning: Can cause an effect that cannot normally be undone.
examples: Permanently deletes or overwrites meaningful data.
Triggers an action whose effect remains after the system state is restored.

sensitivity.label: Public
sensitivity.meaning: Information that does not need confidentiality.
examples: Information intentionally shared with the public.
Information that can be shared without restriction.

sensitivity.label: Routine Internal
sensitivity.meaning: Non-public information whose exposure would have limited impact.
examples: Normal information used for internal work.
Internal descriptive information with little value outside the organization.

sensitivity.label: Internal
sensitivity.meaning: Exposure could cause meaningful harm, but the harm is limited and recoverable.
examples: Internal plans whose exposure could disadvantage the organization.
Internal information whose exposure could cause operational or reputational harm.

sensitivity.label: Confidential
sensitivity.meaning: Exposure could cause serious harm to a person, organization, or its interests.
examples: Sensitive records whose exposure could seriously affect a person.
Non-public information whose exposure could cause major business, legal, financial, or strategic harm.

sensitivity.label: Strictly Confidential
sensitivity.meaning: Exposure could cause severe harm or directly enable unauthorized access, impersonation, fraud, or control.
examples: Secret information that lets someone gain access or authority.
Information whose exposure could cause severe harm to a person or organization.

blast.label: One Item / Person
blast.meaning: The effect stops at one item or person.
examples: One call affects one independent resource.
One person is affected and nothing else depends on the result.

blast.label: One Scope
blast.meaning: The effect stays within one group or scope.
examples: One call affects several resources in one group.
Several users are affected, but all are in the same scope.

blast.label: Multiple Scopes
blast.meaning: One call can affect several separate groups or scopes.
examples: One action affects resources from several groups.
One change affects several separate organizational scopes.

blast.label: Organization-Wide
blast.meaning: One call can affect almost the whole organization.
examples: One action changes a setting used across the organization.
One call affects almost all users or scopes served by the asset.

blast.label: Cascading
blast.meaning: The effect can spread beyond the directly affected scope into other systems or scopes.
examples: A change to one shared dependency affects many dependent systems.
A change to one central resource causes effects across separate systems.

step_prompts.impact: Score the worst reasonable result of **one successful call** using valid inputs. Ask what the call can do — read, change, or destroy. Not how much it touches, and not how valuable the target is; those are the other two steps.
step_prompts.sensitivity: Score how harmful it would be if this information were exposed. Judge what the asset normally holds, in this organization's context. Judge each asset on its own; levels may repeat.
step_prompts.blast: Score how far the result of **one successful call** can reach. Measure reach only — what the asset is worth has already been scored. If a tool cannot affect an asset at all, that pair is marked N/A for you.
step_prompts.inputs:
Each card below is one tool the AI agent can call, with some of its inputs. For every input, decide: could the **value** of this input change the risk of the call **significantly**, for example turn an ordinary call into a high-risk one?

Two example values are shown for each input, only to show what it holds. The agent can send any value.

Some inputs are **ids**. For an id you see only a number or a code, such as `600` or `U01ABCDEF`; you do not know what it points to.

servers.title: Google Calendar
servers.scenario: **Aurora Airways** is a passenger airline. It has to roster crews inside legal working-hour limits, keep its aircraft maintained, and answer to the aviation regulator. Some of what it plans — new routes, aircraft orders — stays commercially sensitive until it is announced.
servers.mcp_context:
**Google Calendar** is where a company keeps its meetings: who is meeting whom, when, where, and about what.

This server lets an AI assistant look through those calendars and add or remove meetings, including inviting people by email.

tools.name: search-events
tools.desc: Returns every event matching a search word, taken from all the calendars the agent can see, with titles and attendees.

tools.name: create-event
tools.desc: Creates a new event, optionally inviting attendees by email.

tools.name: delete-event
tools.desc: Removes an existing event from the calendar.

servers.title: GitHub
servers.scenario: **Helios Grid** runs a country's high-voltage electricity grid, carrying power from the power stations to regional suppliers. About 14 million people depend on it. It is regulated as critical national infrastructure, trades electricity on wholesale markets, and runs the control rooms that switch power in real time.
servers.mcp_context:
**GitHub** is where a company keeps the code its software is built from, and where changes to that code are proposed and checked before they go live.

This server lets an AI assistant read and search the code, write files, and propose and review changes.

tools.name: get_pull_request_files
tools.desc: Returns the names of the files a proposed edit would change, and how many lines change in each.

tools.name: list_pull_requests
tools.desc: Returns a list of the proposed edits to one collection of software, with each one's title, author, and whether it is still open.

tools.name: search_code
tools.desc: Returns lines of software code matching a search word, taken from every collection of code the agent can see.

tools.name: create_or_update_file
tools.desc: Writes one file, creating it or replacing its contents.

tools.name: create_pull_request
tools.desc: Opens a proposed edit to the software so that other people can review it.

tools.name: create_pull_request_review
tools.desc: Records a decision on a proposed edit: approve it, ask for changes, or leave a comment. An approval is the sign-off the edit needs before it can go in.

servers.title: Slack
servers.scenario: **Vireo Bio** is a mid-sized drug company running clinical trials. Its trials are blinded — neither the patients nor the staff know who is getting the real drug and who is getting a dummy one — which is what makes the results trustworthy. It tracks patient safety, deals with the medicines regulator, and analyses the results.
servers.mcp_context:
**Slack** is the chat app a company talks in, split into channels for different teams and topics.

This server lets an AI assistant join and leave channels, read and search what people wrote, and post messages.

tools.name: conversations_join
tools.desc: Adds the agent to a channel, so it can read that channel from then on.

tools.name: conversations_add_message
tools.desc: Posts a message into a channel.

tools.name: conversations_history
tools.desc: Returns the recent messages in one channel.

tools.name: conversations_replies
tools.desc: Returns the replies in one message thread.

tools.name: conversations_search_messages
tools.desc: Returns matching messages from across the workspace.

tools.name: conversations_leave
tools.desc: Removes the agent from a channel, ending its access to that channel.

assets.name: eng-platform
assets.desc: The channel where the engineers who build the trial's data-collection system discuss their work: bugs, releases, and questions about how the system stores data.

assets.name: lab-and-statistics
assets.desc: Chat about lab results, checks that the tests are working properly, and the statistics being run on the trial.

assets.name: regulator-correspondence
assets.desc: Messages about what the company is submitting to the medicines regulator, and what the regulator says back.

assets.name: patient-safety-reports
assets.desc: Reports of patients being harmed during the trial, including details identifying the patient.

assets.name: trial-operations
assets.desc: Running the trial day to day: opening new hospital sites, signing up patients, and problems with following the plan.

assets.name: unblinding-requests
assets.desc: Requests to look up whether a named patient was given the real drug or a dummy one, which is normally recorded but not shown to the study team.

assets.name: announcements
assets.desc: The channel where notices meant for the whole company are posted, such as policy changes and staff news.

servers.title: SQL Database
servers.scenario: **CBG** is a research organisation. It employs staff, wins grants to fund projects, runs experiments that produce data, and publishes papers. Its automated systems sign in to outside services using stored passwords.
servers.mcp_context:
**A database** keeps a company's records in tables — one table for staff, one for projects, and so on, with one row per record.

This server lets an AI assistant see which tables exist, read records out of them, and add or change records.

tools.name: describe_table
tools.desc: Returns the list of headings used by one named table, for example "name", "salary", "start date".

tools.name: list_tables
tools.desc: Returns the names of all the tables of records held in the database.

tools.name: read_query
tools.desc: Returns the entries matching a search the caller writes, which can pull rows from any table in the database.

tools.name: insert_row
tools.desc: Inserts one new row into a named table.

tools.name: write_query
tools.desc: Runs an instruction the caller writes that adds, changes, or deletes entries in the database.

assets.name: api_keys

assets.name: datasets
assets.desc: Research data that has not been published yet, and notes on where it came from.

assets.name: employees
assets.desc: Staff records — name, email, job, department and salary.

assets.name: experiments
assets.desc: A log of experiments that were run: which project, which data, when it started, and how it went.

assets.name: grants
assets.desc: Money awarded to fund research: who gave it, how much, and for how long.

assets.name: projects
assets.desc: The list of research projects — reference number, title, the person leading it, and its start date.

assets.name: publications
assets.desc: Research papers the organisation has already published, with their authors and publication dates.
